_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Cariboo Voices & Local News' — stories FROM and ABOUT the Cariboo-Chilcotin region and its communities. Score 80-100 for articles directly covering: news and events in Williams Lake, Quesnel, 100 Mile House, Bella Coola, Horsefly, Likely, Anahim Lake, Alexis Creek, or the Cariboo Regional District; local government and civic decisions (City of Williams Lake, City of Quesnel, CRD, District of 100 Mile House); local health services and emergency closures; local economy, businesses, and community programs; Cariboo arts, culture, and community events; AND digital equity, rural internet access (fiber, fixed wireless, Starlink), and connectivity serving these specific communities. Articles from local Cariboo news sources (mycariboonow.com, wltribune.com, quesnelobserver.com, 100milefreepress.net, cfjctoday.com) covering Cariboo community life should score 65-85. Score 50-79 for: BC provincial news directly affecting Cariboo communities, rural Canadian community stories closely paralleling Cariboo life, digital equity and rural internet broadly. Score 20-49 for: general BC news that may affect rural areas, broader rural Canada topics without specific Cariboo tie-in. Score 0-19 for: national/international news without Cariboo relevance, pure tech or entertainment with no community angle. Penalise heavily (score 0–20): international geopolitical and war news with no Cariboo tie-in; science discoveries without a local community connection; consumer tech reviews and gadget guides; wildlife and conservation stories not involving Cariboo communities or First Nations; BC provincial news without direct Cariboo-region relevance. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Amid the avalanche of policy announcements, platform promises and attack ads, it can be hard to know where party leaders really stand on the issues. Mario Canseco of Research Co. regularly polls British Columbian voters to ask which issues they care most about. For the past three years, housing has led. This year, it is cost-of-living. In a poll conducted on Oct. 13, the economy/jobs was the top issue for 25 per cent of respondents; housing/poverty/homelessness for 23 per cent; healthcare for 21 per cent, and crime/public safety for nine per cent. With the cost of living the top issue for most voters, economic concerns moved to the forefront as the campaigns hit the home stretch. A back-and-forth emerged as campaigns questioned each other’s math and whether spending or tax-cut promises are realistic. After 10 years in power, the NDP is defending its economic record amid historic deficits. The party’s main new plank is a proposed income tax hike on the wealthiest 3.88 per cent of British Columbians. The NDP says it would spend the extra money on new health-care facilities, child care centres and schools, slowly lowering the deficit over the next three years. The B.C. Conservative Party promises to cut taxes by raising the personal income tax exemption. This would essentially give everyone a $1,000 break. The party also promises new spending and a reduced deficit. items._excerpt: **By Cariboo Gold Dance Band hosting Juno award winning saxophonist Nov. 14** The Cariboo Gold Dance Band asks you to join them on Nov. 14 for "Swing n' Sax" with internationally known and Juno award winning saxophonist Campbell Ryga. A big band in the Williams Lake might seem a bit unusual but the Cariboo Gold Dance Band (CGDB) has been playing together for over 42 years. This 14-piece band, comprised of skilled and dedicated local musicians, played its first dance in the spring of 1984 and has performed for a wide variety of occasions in the Cariboo and beyond ever since. Each year the band brings to the community a professional to work with the CGDB and then perform as a featured artist. This year the dance band will be hosting the triple Juno award recipient and internationally respected saxophone player, Campbell Ryga. Anyone who has enjoyed the music of Michael Bublé and his Grammy winning album, _Crazy Love_, would have heard Campbell’s skillful sax playing. He has also been featured on over 87 other jazz recordings, often as a leader. Most notably, Campbell Ryga is a founding member of the award-winning Hugh Fraser Quintet. British Columbia is full of international acclaimed jazz musicians and Campbell Ryga is no exception. He was born in 1961 in Edmonton but was raised in Summerland, and is the eldest son of renowned author and playwright George Ryga. When he was 18, Ryga moved to Vancouver to pursue advanced musical studies. He has since lived and worked in Vancouver, Toronto, and New York City, establishing an international reputation as both a band leader and creative jazz artist. Ryga is currently based in Kelowna, and serves as a clinician, adjudicator, arts juror and it is a natural fit for him to be the headline performer in the Cariboo Gold Dance Band’s upcoming concert on Saturday, Nov. 14. items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists finally uncover why statins can cause muscle pain
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why statins, the widely prescribed cholesterol-lowering drugs that help prevent heart attacks and strokes, can sometimes cause muscle pain, weakness, and even severe muscle damage. Using advanced imaging technology, researchers discovered that statins can attach to a crucial protein in muscle cells and force open a channel that normally controls calcium flow. This causes calcium to leak continuously, potentially damaging muscle tissue.

Seven-year-old Beckett Tessarolo is “just the happiest kid” – quick with one-liners and always sporting a huge smile, including for his first day of Grade 2 at Crescent Park Elementary when classes resumed in September. Busy with extra-curriculars – as many kids his age are – such as hockey and baseball, it’s hard to believe he started an unimaginable battle for his life just three months shy of his first birthday. “Enough time has passed that you’ll run into people that don’t know he was ever sick,” mom Melanie said in a recent interview. But while Beckett may not remember what led up to his diagnosis with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), nor the eight months he spent in hospital receiving treatment during the initial phase of a clinical trial, his mom’s recollection is crystal clear. “Honestly, everything was scary,” Melanie said. “It’s all so overwhelming.” The “very shocking” diagnosis came soon after Melanie took nine-month-old Becket to the doctor to investigate unusual clinginess and changes to his skin colour. “He was a bit out of sorts and not acting normal,” the South Surrey mom recalled. items.content_html:

In this Brief, Dr. Suzanne Shoush examines how anti-Indigenous bias shapes clinical decision-making and healthcare outcomes, and why public inquests are essential to identifying systemic failures and informing change. Yet, despite decades of documented disparities, the same patterns persist. Addressing them requires moving beyond retrospective investigations to confront the conditions that make these outcomes predictable.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
